articles.title: Treating depression during pregnancy may benefit baby’s brain development – new research
articles.author: Elysia Poggi Davis, Professor of Psychology, University of Denver
paras: Treating pregnant women’s depression with a short course of talk therapy doesn’t just improve their health – it can also shape how their babies’ brains develop before birth. That’s the finding of a new study we co-authored, published in the journal Nature Communications.

The study is part of an ongoing research project that explores how a form of brief interpersonal psychotherapy called MOMCare, which is specially tailored to treating prenatal depression, affects pregnant women with depression and their babies. MOMCare consists of eight 50-minute sessions focused on building interpersonal skills, reducing conflict and strengthening social support.

We enrolled 234 pregnant women who reported having symptoms of depression during their routine prenatal care appointments. Mothers joined the research project during the first or second trimester and were randomly assigned to one of two groups.

Women in one group received MOMCare. Women in the other group received education about mental health, strategies for managing depression symptoms and referrals to mental health support services, such as therapy, in the community. Both groups continued getting their usual medical care, which could also include referrals to therapy or medication.

In a previous publication, we found that 36% of moms enrolled in our study were diagnosed with depression in pregnancy before getting MOMCare and just 6% after it, showing the intervention was effective. Women who received the MOMCare intervention were also more likely to carry their baby to term, which is linked with shorter hospital stays after birth and improvements in many aspects of child health and development, including better school performance.

In the current study, to investigate how this form of talk therapy affects a baby’s developing brain, we measured the volume of different brain areas using an imaging technique called magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, within a few weeks of birth. We found that a brain area called the hippocampus, which plays a role in learning, memory and emotional regulation, was 5% smaller by volume in infants whose mothers received MOMCare compared to mothers in the other group.

Six months later, we brought the babies back into the lab to examine their emotional responses to unfamiliar experiences, such as encountering a noisy toy robot that danced and moved unpredictably. According to earlier studies, babies who respond more negatively to these tasks have higher levels of depression and anxiety in adolescence.
In our study, we found that babies with a smaller hippocampal volume at birth tended to respond less negatively than those with larger volume.

It may seem counterintuitive that a smaller brain volume is associated with stronger emotional regulation, particularly since in adults smaller brain volume is often associated with negative effects. However, in infancy the brain is growing, and faster growth may not always be advantageous. For example, one hypothesis proposes that stress can accelerate early brain development.

Depression affects up to 1 in 5 women during pregnancy. It also raises the risk of pregnancy complications such as high blood pressure and preterm birth. And having depression during pregnancy raises the risk of mental illness in the child.

Pregnancy offers a unique opportunity to simultaneously improve the health of both mother and baby. This is because women often have more contact with the healthcare system during pregnancy than at other times in their lives. Treating a woman’s depression during her pregnancy benefits two generations, improving the health of the mother and her developing baby.

Even though both MOMCare and the control condition in our study provided more support than pregnant women experiencing symptoms of depression often receive, we still saw a big difference between the groups. This suggests that a targeted intervention, even a noninvasive and relatively low-cost one such as MOMCare, can make a big difference.

Our study is the first to show that treating a woman’s depression during pregnancy may influence infant brain development. It aligns with a small but growing number of randomized clinical trials showing that reducing maternal depression has benefits for babies, including improved emotional development and changes in stress-related hormones.

These findings, if confirmed, could explain the biological underpinnings behind why treating prenatal depression is so critical. Further, they support public health initiatives to increase accessible mental health support during pregnancy.

It’s not clear how lessening mom’s depression in pregnancy leads to changes in the baby’s brain. It’s possible, for example, that stress-related hormones or inflammation associated with depression could influence brain growth.

Another open question is how the brain changes we observed might affect babies’ development long term. We hope to address this by continuing to follow mothers and babies through early childhood. By tracking conditions such as depression and anxiety as the children get older, we hope to determine whether treating mothers’ depression in pregnancy has lasting benefits for their children’s mental health and well-being.
The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
articles.author: Jaquelyn Jahn, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology, Drexel University
paras: When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons.

Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.”

I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years.

While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons.

Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme. Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs, Dallas, Laurel Highlands, Muncy, Waymart and Huntingdon, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.
Prison healthcare systems under strain

Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease, and the state’s prison population is getting older, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023.
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year. That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults.

The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.

Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers.

In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour.
Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks

One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men.

This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.

Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “accelerated aging” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected.
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable.
Preparing for a warmer climate

Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.

articles.title: Can social media bans protect young people’s mental health? Early research suggests that bans aren’t the answer
articles.author: Ari Lightman, Professor of Digital Media and Marketing, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: The year 2026 has been an expensive one for social media platforms.

Since March, YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, have settled or paid out in multiple lawsuits to the tune of more than US$17 billion for allegedly acting negligently, deliberately designing their platforms to hook kids and misleading the public about safety and privacy. If these suits are any indication of how states and the public are starting to view social media platforms, more may follow.

On top of these lawsuits, social media platforms are facing a loss of business as bans for minors are accelerating and spreading worldwide. Australia was one of the first with a ban on kids under 16 on social media starting in December 2025, followed soon after by the U.K. with a similar prohibition.

The current list of countries looking to ban minors from these platforms tops more than 20, from Greece to the United Arab Emirates to Canada. The proposed and enacted bans around the world vary in terms of age restriction, parental consent rules and age verification methods. Different countries are looking at restricting different platforms, but most include a mix of Snapchat, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X.

These bans aren’t necessarily for mental health reasons only – some are motivated by political concerns about foreign-owned platforms, and others aim to protect young people’s privacy. But nearly every government banning social media platforms for young people mentions their mental health as a reason.

The question is, are these bans the solution to the mental health problems young people are facing? I research digital media and marketing and measure the impact of new technologies, and I’m skeptical about whether prohibiting access to these platforms will actually improve young people’s mental health.

Since Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book “The Anxious Generation” critics of social media have increasingly focused on young people’s mental health. Haidt argues that social media disrupts kids’ social and neurological development, contributing to rising anxiety and depression through sleep loss, fragmented attention, addiction, loneliness, social comparison and perfectionism.
A 2026 study found that young people between 14 and 20 are more than 100% more likely to experience mental illness than 14- to 20-year-olds 50 years ago.

Increased use of social media and screen time is compounding an already precarious time for minors. In 2021 it was estimated that 20.5% of young people experienced elevated symptoms of anxiety, and 25.2% of youth reported elevated symptoms of depression globally.

Many factors contribute to this, including better screening and awareness of kids’ mental health problems, as well as societal disruptions as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. As the world sheltered in place and moved online for work, school and social interactions, there was an increase in isolation and loneliness.
In light of these concerns, some researchers argue that bans on social media platforms are like putting an age restriction on buying alcohol or cigarettes.

But unlike these addictive and potentially harmful substances, there are benefits to social media, especially for teens who feel disconnected from their local communities and want to build relationships with others who feel similarly.
Social media platforms allow for global connectivity and community-building with like-minded groups. They also provide a place for self-expression and civic engagement.
In a Pew survey of U.S. teens, 80% said social media helps them stay connected to what’s happening in their friends’ lives.
One place where the comparison with tobacco is actually quite apt is in relation to the money from lawsuit settlements.

In 1998, states settled a lawsuit against the major tobacco companies to recover smoking-related healthcare costs. Part of the settlement was allocated to programs aimed at reducing youth smoking. In 2026, total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.

Similarly, some money from an August 2026 Meta settlement with a group of states for $17 billion is slated for state-based programs focusing on mental health infrastructure, school and community programs, and public health campaigns.
However, there is no oversight or direction as to how states should use the funds, nor is there a mechanism to report how that money has improved kids’ mental health care, safety and well-being.

Early evidence from the Australian social media ban shows that kids are finding work-arounds: Roughly 61% of kids ages 12–15 continue to access platforms using false IDs, altered appearances or virtual private networks, or VPNs, even though millions of accounts were disabled. In fact, this has become so common that U.K. lawmakers are debating restricting consumer VPN access.

Some countries, such as Australia, require the platforms themselves to develop ways of verifying a user’s age. Some minors have bypassed scans from biometric age estimation technology by using photo manipulation software, substituting celebrity photos, using clever makeup and even utilizing older friends and parents to pass the “selfie tests” on their behalf. Others simply manipulate their birth years during registration or rely on existing adult-verified accounts managed by family members.
And all of these age-verification methods, whether developed by a government or a social media platform, rely on collecting sensitive data to estimate age accurately, which creates privacy concerns.

Australia is currently seeking to raise fines on social media platforms that fail to comply with its requirements. The Australian safety commissioner, charged with enforcing the ban, issued a compliance update that showed 7 in 10 children who held accounts in restricted platforms remained on those platforms, and more than 80% of Australian teens ages 10-15 still use social media frequently.
Beyond concerns about enacting and enforcing these restrictions, some policymakers also worry that total bans could push some kids to migrate to even riskier online spaces.
Based on the evidence, I’m not convinced that banning social media platforms will be an effective solution to the mental health crisis among young people today.
Supporting young people’s mental health is a complex endeavor that will require a combination of people, organizations and resources coming together.

I believe kids’ mental health would be better served by governments enforcing safety by default standards on social media platforms rather than outright bans. This means that the highest security and privacy options are in place by default so that minors still on a platform are protected. For instance, accounts would be unsearchable by default, so users would have to intentionally make a profile change to be found by people they don’t know in real life.

Safety by default standards also place limits on the manipulation, algorithmic restraint and other addictive mechanisms that may lead to psychological harm in vulnerable populations such as young people.
Educating kids on digital literacy and online safety as well as ensuring some screen-free time are also going to help support kids’ mental health.

It’s also important for parents and other caregivers to recognize changes in behavior as a result of addiction to social platforms and screens. And when adults start seeing signs of a problem, they need clear, easy and affordable ways to connect their kids to mental health support, which is not available in most places right now.

And finally, the United Nations recommends bringing kids into the conversation about what’s best for them online. Obviously, this does not mean putting 12-year-olds in charge of regulatory agencies. But feedback from young people about what they care about, what they get out of being online and what makes it hard for them to look away from their screens could inform changes to social media platforms and education programs that could help young people engage online more safely and maintain a healthy balance.
Ari Lightman is affiliated with Jewish Healthcare Foundation

articles.title: Ketamine’s role in alleged Cornell rape highlights flood of psychoactive drugs on campus
articles.author: Christopher P. Holstege, Professor of Emergency Medicine and Pediatrics, University of Virginia
paras: Former Cornell student Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026 alleging that seven fraternity members raped her at a party, said the young men who assaulted her pressured her into taking the drug ketamine.

As an emergency room physician, medical toxicologist and the head of student health services at the University of Virginia, I have had a front-row seat to the growing danger that psychoactive substances such as ketamine present to the health and safety of university students.

Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions are part of a wave of new and evolving designer drugs entering the United States and other countries. How widely these substances are used remains unknown, since most hospitals are unable to detect them on standard urine drug screens. But ketamine and other drugs are being increasingly reported as agents used in sexual assault – either when people take these drugs voluntarily, are pressured to take them or are given them covertly.
The increasing prevalence of ketamine and other drugs – and their use in sexual assault – is playing out on college campuses across the U.S. and putting students at risk.

Ketamine is a synthetic chemical that was first synthesized in 1962. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it as a general anesthetic for people and animals in 1970, and doctors and veterinarians used it for decades to induce anesthesia during surgeries and to relieve pain.

People have used ketamine recreationally since the 1970s. Getting high on it became more popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, when it was called “Special K.” It was frequently found in the club drug scenes and was associated with raves into the 1990s. Today, ketamine is sold on the street under a variety of slang names, such as K, Ket, and Vitamin K.

In 2019, the FDA approved a nasal spray version of ketamine, called esketamine, to treat depression that does not respond to other treatments. That drug’s use is tightly regulated, but clinicians are increasingly prescribing ketamine “off-label” for a variety of psychiatric conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder.

Cases of poisoning caused by ketamine in the U.S. doubled between 2019 and 2023, according to an analysis of calls to poison control centers nationwide, and are now the highest they’ve ever been. This surge is in part due to the more widespread medical use of ketamine, which makes accessing it much easier. But street versions of the drug are also prevalent as chemists in basement laboratories create novel ketamine analogs.
Ketamine’s effects on the body

Ketamine’s effects vary depending on the dose and the person. It can cause someone to dissociate, creating an altered state of consciousness, changing what’s perceived through the senses and causing a sense of detachment from one’s self and one’s surroundings. The drug can also cause coma at high doses.

Someone who orally consumes ketamine would typically begin to feel its effects within 20 minutes. If they inhale or inject it, the effects are almost immediate. The primary effects generally wear off in less than an hour, but a person’s senses may remain dulled and their judgment and coordination impaired for several hours afterward.

Ketamine can cause a slew of other side effects, including delirium, amnesia, increased salivation, abnormal eye movements, high blood pressure and potentially fatal breathing problems. Alcohol and other drugs can interact with ketamine to worsen these effects significantly.

Ketamine is generally sold illegally as either a colorless, odorless liquid or a white or off-white powder. Either form can be easily and covertly placed into an unsuspecting person’s beverage or food. Ketamine can be snorted, and it can be smoked or vaped on products such as marijuana.
Ketamine and other drugs in sexual assault

Research is extremely spotty on how often a perpetrator of rape or sexual assault uses a chemical agent – whether ketamine, alcohol or another substance – to alter a victim’s senses. Research suggests that most often both parties use mind-altering substances voluntarily, although the effects of these substances can alter a person’s ability to grant consent.

Even so, there are numerous reports of perpetrators spiking a victim’s drink or otherwise slipping a drug to them without their knowledge. According to one study, 4.2% of rape victims were drugged covertly, though how often this actually happens is undoubtedly underreported.

That’s because it’s very hard to detect drugs taken this way. Most of the substances used to facilitate sexual assaults are rapidly absorbed and metabolized by the body, rendering them difficult to detect in routine urine and blood drug screenings. Another issue is that many days may have elapsed between the victim ingesting the drugs and their subsequent treatment at a medical facility.

Victims of rape or sexual assault are often reluctant to report incidents because of a sense of embarrassment, guilt or perceived responsibility, or because they may know their attacker. Some may not trust that their institution or local law enforcement will support them.

In my experience, the involvement of ketamine or other drugs invariably makes a bad situation worse – complicating consent, impairing judgment and reducing inhibitions. Ketamine causes confusion and drowsiness, and its sedative, hypnotic and memory-erasing properties can diminish a survivor’s recollection of events surrounding the sexual assault.

The availability of these drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has risen sharply – particularly since the early 2010s, as a slew of new substances have emerged and international drug control efforts have not kept up. Without more active education and prevention efforts, as well as better detection methods for these drugs, students will continue to pay the price.

articles.title: Cystic fibrosis patients got their ‘miracle drug’ thanks to federal research funding – new Trump administration rules may cut future miracles short
articles.author: Fred D. Ledley, Director, Center for Integration of Science and Industry, Bentley University
paras: The hardest disease to care for when I was training as a pediatrician in the late 1970s was cystic fibrosis, a disease in which abnormally thick mucus secretions block the lungs’ airways and make it progressively harder to breathe.

Back then, there was no treatment for the disease itself. All we had was physical therapy to clear mucus from the lungs, and drugs to dilate the airways and aid breathing. We used high doses of antibiotics to treat chronic pneumonia – drugs that also generated dangerous antibiotic-resistant infections that not only made the disease progressively harder to treat but also posed a threat to other people. At the same time, we also had to manage co-occurring conditions, including diabetes, malnutrition and heart failure.

Worse, these efforts did not work. In 1979 the median age of death from cystic fibrosis was 15. While all young deaths are tragic, caring for children with a progressive, inevitably fatal disease that denied emerging adolescents the promise of adulthood was especially heartbreaking.

Cystic fibrosis treatment changed dramatically after 2012, when the biotech company Vertex Pharmaceuticals launched the drug Kalydeco (ivacaftor), followed by additional cystic fibrosis drugs Orkambi (lumacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2015, Symdeko (tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2018, Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) in 2019 and Alyftrek (vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor) in 2024.

Now, the median survival age for a child with cystic fibrosis born today in the United States is 66 years. Mary Vought, the former wife of the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, stated that their daughter, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, “can live likely a full life because of this miracle drug,” and that “it is very, very, very hopeful.”

Cystic fibrosis treatments are not miracles; they required decades of research funded by a combination of public and private investments. The largest contributor to this work was the National Institutes of Health, which funded much of the pivotal research required to understand the genetics and biology of the disease. Only with this knowledge was it possible to begin searching for drugs to treat cystic fibrosis.

Ironically, the federal funding that was so critical to developing these drugs is now threatened by policies that were initially proposed by the Office of Management and Budget. Those policies, which would increase political control over federal research grants, limit peer review and curtail research on certain topics, were temporarily blocked by Congress. But several federal agencies are still pursing portions of this agenda, including the NIH.
NIH laid the foundation for treatment

My colleagues and I examined the role that federal funding from the National Institutes of Health has played in developing cystic fibrosis treatments. We found that NIH funding supported more than 6,200 published research papers on the biology of cystic fibrosis in the 27 years before Kalydeco was approved in 2012.

Some of these publications describe celebrated milestones in understanding the biology of CFTR – the gene that causes cystic fibrosis – or the disease process. Others describe the studies necessary to replicate, refute or refine these advances and ensure the necessary scientific rigor to successfully discover and develop new drugs.

Overall, we identified US$3.2 billion in NIH funding for basic research on cystic fibrosis from 1985 to 2012 and approximately $940 million in funding for applied research on potential drugs. This funding complemented at least $200 million in investments from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for the discovery or development of these drugs as well as undisclosed spending by Vertex to develop and commercialize these products.

The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation acknowledged the essential role of the NIH in a 2025 letter to Russell Vought and other Trump administration leaders, writing that “ensuring that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) is fully functional is critical for furthering our knowledge of the biology of CF and advancing CF therapeutic development.”
What will it take to produce future miracles?
Developing groundbreaking drugs requires a long-term, sustained commitment from the public, from the government and from industry.

FDA-approved drugs are typically based on 20 to 30 years of basic research in the lab and eight to nine years of human testing in the clinic. This work is supported, at least in part, by an average of $1.4 billion in NIH funding and as much as a reported $1.4 billion in industry funding per drug.

Russell Vought and his family have benefited from the commitment that scientists, advocates, legislators and industry leaders have placed into developing treatments that now offer patients with cystic fibrosis a normal life. A similar commitment can help find cures for patients who don’t respond to available drugs and to provide cures for cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia and other conditions.

This commitment to research is currently under threat from Trump administration proposals that would reduce NIH funding, research, training and global research collaboration. Protecting or expanding federal funding for basic research instead can help lead to innovative therapies for countless patients.

Fred D. Ledley has received research funding for related research from the National Biomedical Research Foundation, Institute for New Economic Thinking, West Health, and the National Pharmaceutical Council.

articles.title: I’m a pediatrician and a mom - here’s how to treat lice without stigma
articles.author: Emily J. C. Wong, Associate Professor of Pediatrics, University of Virginia
paras: Four words that parents in the classroom group chat dread to read: ‘My kid has lice.’

Head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis) are parasites that primarily infest children in childcare, preschool or elementary school. Having lice doesn’t indicate poor hygiene, despite a longstanding misconception driven by stigma, and lice don’t spread other diseases. But children with lice are often shamed and unnecessarily excluded from attending school.

As a primary care pediatrician with specialized training in infections and infestations of microbes, viruses and tiny pests such as lice, my goal is to keep children healthy so that they can stay in school. And as a mother of two, I personally have experienced the battle against lice with my own children.

Head lice have been humans’ unwanted companions since ancient times. Understanding how they spread, as well as how to detect and treat infestations, can help parents and schools handle head lice effectively without fear.

Adult head lice are gray-tan insects with six legs, approximately 2-3 millimeters long – about the size of a sesame seed. They live exclusively on humans, feeding on blood by biting the scalp and using their saliva to prevent the blood from coagulating.
Female lice lay eggs on hair close to the scalp, attaching the eggs firmly to the hair shaft with a secreted glue-like substance. The eggs take 8 to 9 days to hatch.

Since head lice cannot jump or fly, they most often spread from person to person through direct head-to-head contact. In school, this might happen when children are sitting very close to each other or napping alongside classmates. Eggs or lice can also be spread when kids share objects like hats or hair brushes, but this route is much less common because they don’t live long off of the head.
There is no medical evidence that certain types of hair are resistant. Lice can infest all hair types.

Your child might have lice if you see them frequently scratching their scalp. That itchiness is a sensitivity reaction most children develop to lice saliva. It can take four to six weeks for the sensitization to develop in children who have never had lice before – which means your child has likely had lice for a few weeks by the time you discover them.
what to do if you think your child has head lice
First of all, don’t panic. A head lice infestation can be frustrating or embarrassing, but it’s not dangerous and there are effective treatments.

Look closely at your child’s scalp for live lice. They move fast and avoid light, so it might be difficult to find one. Be sure to check for eggs, which are often behind the ears or at the nape of the neck. Eggs are securely attached to hair and not flaky like dandruff.

Once you are sure your child has head lice, check other household members, too. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that you treat all household members who have lice, as well as anyone who shares a bed with the child, even if you don’t find lice or eggs on them.
Several treatment options exist that are approved by the Food and Drug Administration, safe for children, available over the counter and affordable:

1% permethrin is available as a lotion or a cream rinse and sold under the brand name Nix in the U.S. as well as in generic forms. It can be used for children 2 months and older. It kills live lice effectively but not eggs, so you’ll need to reapply it in nine to 10 days to kill any lice that may have hatched since the first treatment.

Pyrethrins + piperonyl butoxide shampoo is sold under the brand name Rid and in generic form. This substance can be used for children 24 months and older. Like 1% permethrin, it generally needs to be reapplied nine to 10 days after first use.

Ivermectin 0.5% lotion can be used for kids older than 6 months. In addition to killing adult lice, ivermectin continues to kill new lice that hatch after treatment, so a single application should do the job.

After the topical treatment, comb the hair with a fine-toothed comb to ensure that no live lice remain. Using a creamy conditioner as you comb can make lice more visible. Since no treatment is 100% effective, combing also helps to remove eggs that would later hatch into live lice and would need to be killed with the second treatment. Getting rid of the empty nits isn’t necessary, but it can reduce a child’s embarrassment and parental worry.
What if treatment doesn’t work?

An itchy head after topical treatment may just be a reaction to the treatment itself. Check for live lice or new eggs, which would be sitting within 1-2 millimeters of the hair base, rather than empty nits that are whiter and farther along the hair shaft.

Sometimes over-the-counter treatments don’t work fully – either due to user error or re-exposure, or because the lice have developed a resistance to them. If you have the resources, lice removal salons or clinics – available in most urban and suburban areas – can offer professional help. Alternatively, you should be able to get one of these second-line therapies, available by prescription only, from your child’s healthcare provider:

Malathion 0.5% lotion is sold as brand-name Ovide or as a generic form and approved for children age 6 and older. Because malathion is highly flammable, you cannot expose the treated hair to any heat, even a hair dryer. If you see live lice in seven to nine days, repeat the treatment.
Spinosad 0.9% suspension is available as the brand-name Natroba or as a generic liquid. You can apply it on children 6 months and older. Repeat the treatment if you see live lice in seven days.

Ivermectin oral tablets are approved to treat lice in adults, but not in children. However, since oral ivermectin is approved in children for other parasitic infections who weigh at least 33 lbs, doctors can use it to treat lice off-label.

If you would prefer to avoid chemical treatment, you can try manually removing every single louse and using an emollient with dimethicone lotion. However, research on whether this technique is effective is limited. And none of the many alternative remedies for treating lice – such as smothering them with mayonnaise or oil, dehydrating them with saline or hot air, or zapping them with an electronic comb – have proven to be effective.

Lice do not survive more than 48 hours off the head. To kill lice or eggs that have jumped to surfaces, wash all clothing, bedding, head wear and toys that came in contact with the child’s head in the past two days in hot water and dry them on high heat. Vacuum furniture and carpets to remove hair, and place any objects that cannot be washed in plastic bags for two weeks.
What about school attendance?

Beginning in the 1980’s, as an effort to contain outbreaks of head lice, many schools in the United States adopted “No Nit” policies that excluded children from attendance if any eggs or empty nits were found on the child’s head.

However, many medical experts and public health organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, reject these policies as unnecessary and ineffective. Keeping children out of school due to lice also contributes to social stigma.

According to current guidelines, if a child has a head lice infestation, they should not be sent home early from school. Instead, the school should notify parents, and the child should keep attending school as they are being treated. They should also avoid close head contact and sharing items like hats, scarves and hairbrushes.
Some schools continue to check students’ hair for nits after treatment, but this practice is not effective since empty nits without live lice can persist in hair for weeks or even months.
Emily J. Wong is affiliated with the American Academy of Pediatrics. She receives funding from the American Academy of Pediatrics.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer highlights growing number of nonsmokers diagnosed with the disease – and younger people too
articles.author: Estelamari Rodriguez, Associate Director of Community Outreach in Thoracic Oncology, University of Miami
paras: When many people think of an average lung cancer patient, they often imagine an older man smoking. But the face of lung cancer has changed. Over the past 15 years, more women, never smokers and younger people are being diagnosed with lung cancer.

In fact, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women, and more women die from lung cancer than breast, ovarian and colorectal cancer each year. The American Lung Association reports that while lung cancer rates have risen by 79% for women over the last 44 years, they decreased by 43% for men. And for the first time in history, there are more young women than men diagnosed with lung cancer.

News about Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis on Oct. 13, 2026, sparked discussion about increasing rates of the disease among people who have never smoked. Leo reportedly is not a smoker. Potential causes for the disease include environmental exposures and genetics, and recognizing the diverse factors that can increase someone’s risk of lung cancer – regardless of their smoking history – is essential for timely and appropriate screening and treatment.

Cancer that is found at the earliest stages, like that of the pope, can be treated with surgery and cured for both smokers and nonsmokers. The challenge is that people who have never smoked are not currently included in lung cancer screening guidelines, and tumors are often only found by chance.

As a thoracic oncologist, I have seen many younger women and never smokers walk into my clinic with a new diagnosis of lung cancer. Particularly for never smokers, lung cancer is unexpected for both patients and their doctors, which can often lead to delays in diagnosis. Researchers have described this trend of increasing lung cancer rates among women in different parts of the world and are starting to understand why cases are on the rise.
The first explanation of why rates of lung cancer in women have increased is that many started smoking later than men, pushing back their peak in smoking-related lung cancer diagnoses.

Women also started smoking in the years when filtered cigarettes were most commonly used. This led to an increased risk of a type of cancer called adenocarcinoma due to the way cigarette filters distribute tobacco smoke to the outer parts of the lungs. Some studies suggest that women are more susceptible to the carcinogenic effects of exposure to tobacco and cigarette smoke, including second-hand smoke, and may develop lung cancer after fewer years of smoking compared to men.

However, it is important to note that most people diagnosed today with lung cancer are not active smokers. About 20% of women with lung cancer have never smoked – higher than for men with lung cancer who’ve never smoked.
Besides smoking and secondhand smoke, there are several other lung cancer risk factors. These include a family history of cancer and exposure to asbestos, radon and air pollution.

Exposure to carcinogens in the workplace in the form of inhaled chemicals such as arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, silica and nickel is still a concern in some parts of the world. The potential lung cancer risk of e-cigarette and marijuana smoke is still under study but of potential concern.

Recently, researchers have also found that genetics can play a role in lung cancer risk in some patients with a strong history of lung cancer. Studies of these families have helped identify potential susceptibility genes for lung cancer and environmental risk factors.

Like BRCA1 and BRCA2 in breast cancer, alterations in genes that promote or protect against tumor development can contribute to lung cancer development. Researchers have yet to identify specific mutations that may predispose individuals to lung cancer. However, studying familial genetic predispositions can help elucidate how lung cancer develops and lead to new biomarkers for early cancer detection in high-risk groups.

In 2021, the United States Preventive Services Task Force updated its lung cancer screening guidelines to include younger patients with less smoking history. Now, lung cancer screening is recommended for adults ages 50 to 80 who have smoked at least one pack per day for 20 years, current smokers and former smokers who quit smoking within the last 15 years. Women at risk for lung cancer can talk to their doctors about ordering a low-dose CT scan for lung cancer screening.

Nationwide, more than 70% of eligible women undergo breast cancer screening but less than 6% of all eligible smokers pursue lung cancer screening. Researchers estimate that these new screening guidelines will increase the number of women eligible for lung cancer screening by 40% by including those at a younger age who have less smoking exposure.

In recent years, increasing understanding of the genetic changes that can lead to cancer and how to harness the immune system to treat cancer has led to new targeted therapies and immunotherapies that have improved the prognosis of patients with lung cancer. Women tend to have a better lung cancer prognosis than men, especially if they never smoked and have tumors with molecular changes that can be treated with targeted therapies.

However, lung cancer symptoms may go unrecognized in women. Symptoms of lung cancer can include coughing, shortness of breath, overwhelming fatigue and pain in the back, chest or shoulder, which could be confused for other ailments. Because women tend to be slightly younger when diagnosed than men, patients may be able to tolerate symptoms longer and delay seeking medical attention. Physicians also might not attribute these symptoms to lung cancer due to a patient’s younger age.

Recognizing the early symptoms of lung cancer, expanding lung cancer screening eligibility and testing for genetic biomarkers to select the best therapy are some of the steps that could help address the global epidemic of lung cancer in women.
This is an updated version of an article published on Feb. 1, 2023.
Estelamari Rodriguez is affiliated with University of Miami Health System. She receives funding from the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Nicotine pouches, vaping or cigarettes: Which nicotine product is actually the least harmful?
articles.author: Emma Fenske, Assistant Professor of Medicine, Addiction Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz; Oregon Health & Science University
paras: “Do you smoke cigarettes?” I asked my patient succinctly in a recent clinic appointment.
He matter-of-factly responded, “Not anymore, I use Zyn pouches now.”
As with any patient, I gauged his readiness – or reluctance, in some instances – to disrupt his use of nicotine.
I asked about his interest in trying nicotine replacement therapy, a medical treatment that provides low, controlled amounts of nicotine. Initially, his response caught me by surprise.
“Aren’t I already using nicotine replacement products?” he asked astutely.

I gathered my thoughts and explained that while nicotine pouches are indeed a form of nicotine replacement, there are important caveats. Actual nicotine replacement therapy products are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration to help people quit smoking. In contrast, I explained that Zyn and other nicotine pouches are commercial tobacco products that are regulated by the FDA but are not FDA-approved smoking cessation medications.

My patient was surprised, because he had not realized there was a difference, which is a common misunderstanding. This encounter proved pivotal in the direction I would take in my subsequent clinical encounters.
As an addiction medicine physician, I often talk with patients who use nicotine in various forms.
Understanding how these products differ and what we know about their relative risks can help people make more informed choices.
Doing away with good/bad thinking
One of the most important distinctions I make when I talk to patients is distinguishing between the harms caused by nicotine itself and the harms caused by the way it is delivered.
Combustible tobacco products such as cigarettes expose users to thousands of chemicals produced by burning tobacco, while newer products such as vapes deliver nicotine without combustion.

But the lack of combustion does not make the newer products inherently safe. Nicotine remains addictive, and studies have raised concerns about its cardiovascular effects, including changes in heart rate, blood pressure and underlying vascular function.
The long-term health effects of newer nicotine products – particularly nicotine pouches – are not yet well established.

As a result, discussions about which nicotine product is appropriate for a given person do not fall into categories of “good” or “bad.” Rather, they involve nuanced conversations with patients to help them reach their goals and reduce overall harm.

What’s more, the health implications of a nicotine product depend not only on what is in it, but also on who is using it, how they use it and what it replaces. Relative harms vary significantly when talking about a current tobacco smoker who switches to an e-cigarette compared with a nonsmoker who starts vaping. The same distinction matters for nicotine pouches: Their lower exposure to many toxic chemicals does not make them risk-free, particularly for adolescents and other nonsmokers who have not previously used nicotine.
In 1965, 42.4% of the U.S. population smoked. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 11.6%.

This dramatic decline did not happen because of a single intervention, but through decades of accumulating scientific evidence, public education campaigns, warning labels, restrictions on advertising, smoke-free policies, higher tobacco taxes and shifts in social norms. At the same time, the tobacco landscape has evolved, with noncombustible nicotine products such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches becoming increasingly prominent.

In the U.S., 6.5% of adults reported using e-cigarettes in 2023, while past-year nicotine pouch use rose from 3.4% in 2023 to 5.9% in 2024. This fast-growing trend makes it clear that the public is in need of a better understanding of the relative harms of nicotine products.
To be clear, the major source of cigarette-related harm is burning tobacco, not simply the presence of nicotine.
Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which are toxic and carcinogenic, culminating in approximately 2.5 million cancer deaths per year worldwide.
Patients also often land in the hospital with complications related to tobacco use, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cardiovascular disease.
While nicotine itself is the reason for dependence, the toxic mixture generated by burning tobacco leaves is what makes cigarette smoking so extraordinarily harmful.
Nicotine products compared
So, where do vaping, heated tobacco – also known as “heat-not-burn products” – cigarettes and oral nicotine fall on the spectrum of safety?

Electronic cigarettes – or vapes – generally contain fewer and lower levels of many toxic chemicals compared with cigarette smoke. However, inhaled aerosols can still contain harmful substances such as propylene glycol, which is often found in certain medicines, cosmetics and food products. While propylene glycol is classified as “generally safe” by the FDA for use in food, that designation does not establish that it is safe to inhale. The lungs process substances differently from the digestive system, and the health effects of chronic inhalation of propylene glycol through e-cigarette aerosol remain incompletely understood.

Heated tobacco products such as processed tobacco sticks, loose-leaf chambers, tobacco capsules and pods, or carbon-tipped pods typically heat tobacco to lower temperatures as opposed to burning it. This can lead to lower exposure to harmful substances compared with conventional cigarettes. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers any tobacco product harmful, given that these products still deliver tobacco-derived nicotine and other toxins.

An increasingly prominent product is the nicotine pouch, such as the brand-name product Zyn. Sales of nicotine pouches in the U.S. have increased substantially in recent years, particularly since 2023. Unlike traditional smokeless tobacco, nicotine pouches contain no tobacco leaf; instead, they contain nicotine, flavorings and other ingredients. Users typically place a pouch between the upper lip and gum, where nicotine is absorbed through the tissues of the mouth.

Nicotine pouches generally result in lower exposure to many toxic substances, given that there is no combustion or inhaled aerosols. However, they can deliver substantial amounts of nicotine. Depending on the product, a single pouch may contain several milligrams of nicotine – comparable to or exceeding the amount of nicotine you would otherwise get from a cigarette. These products therefore remain addictive.
With all nicotine products, the relevant comparison is not “safe” versus “dangerous,” but rather “more harmful” versus “less harmful.
FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapy

Nicotine replacement therapy, on the other hand, is an FDA-approved medical treatment that delivers controlled, low amounts of nicotine without the many carcinogens and toxic chemicals found in tobacco smoke. These products come in the form of patches, gum, lozenges, nasal sprays and inhalers, intended to reduce cravings and withdrawal while helping people gradually move away from tobacco use.

Unlike nicotine replacement therapies, which are FDA-approved and supported by strong evidence of effectiveness for smoking cessation, e-cigarettes are not FDA-approved cessation treatments, despite evidence that they can help some people quit smoking. Evidence for nicotine pouches as a cessation aid remains limited, and they have not been FDA-approved for this purpose.
Patterns of nicotine and tobacco use also vary considerably across countries and populations, reflecting differences in culture, tobacco-control policies, product availability and patterns of use.

Similarly, access to smoking-cessation treatment and harm-reduction resources varies substantially from country to country. In the U.K., for example, cessation services are integrated into the country’s National Health Service, while Australia provides state-based "Quit” line services and permits regulated access to some nicotine vaping products through pharmacies. Many countries have limited or no comprehensive services focused on smoking cessation, and access to medications such as nicotine replacement therapy remains uneven.
Putting nicotine risk in perspective

For people who do not use nicotine, there is little reason to start. For people who smoke, quitting remains the best option. But if quitting is not immediately achievable, moving away from combustible tobacco may reduce exposure to harmful chemicals in cigarette smoke.

The goal is not to label every nicotine product “good” or “bad,” but to help people understand the trade-offs – and to make choices that move them toward less harm and, ultimately, away from nicotine dependence.

articles.title: That brightly packaged sexual enhancement pill at the gas station might be laced with dangerous drugs
articles.author: Andrew Yockey, Assistant Professor of Health and Kinesiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: Brightly colored packaging, promises of better sexual performance and names like “Rhino,” “Anaconda” and “Magnum” make sexual enhancement products difficult to miss. They can be found online, in convenience stores and at gas stations, and some can even be ordered through delivery services.
But what’s inside the package may be considerably different from what appears on the label.

In May 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration warned consumers not to use a sexual enhancement product called Rhino 7S Type F3 7000, one of many Rhino-branded products. Laboratory testing had found that it contained two ingredients that did not appear on its label: sildenafil – the active ingredient in the prescription erectile dysfunction medication Viagra – and acetaminophen, the widely used pain reliever also sold as Tylenol.
This finding was not an isolated incident.
Dating back to 2007, the FDA has maintained an expanding list of health fraud scams, including sexual enhancement and energy products found to contain hidden pharmaceutical ingredients.

Today, the sexual enhancement market is still going strong – and still putting out adulterated substances. Seven new products were added to the FDA’s list in September 2026. Recent warnings have involved pills, gummies, honey products, coffee and even chocolates marketed as sexual enhancers.

As a public health researcher who studies substance use and health behaviors with unregulated products, I see these products as part of a larger challenge created by global supply chains, online commerce and a regulatory system that struggles to keep pace with rapidly changing products.
Supplements are regulated – but not like prescription drugs

In the U.S., the FDA regulates dietary supplements under a different framework than for prescription and over-the-counter drugs. Those drugs undergo a rigorous application process involving three phases of trials that usually take nearly a decade to complete.

Supplements, on the other hand, are regulated under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, which holds manufacturers responsible for ensuring that their supplements are safe and properly labeled. So dietary supplements aren’t completely unregulated, but they generally do not go through the FDA’s premarket approval process. This means the FDA does not approve them for safety and effectiveness before they reach consumers, as it does with medications.

That creates an important distinction between pharmaceutical drugs like Viagra and products marketed as dietary supplements, such as many Rhino-branded sexual enhancement products. Viagra is an FDA-approved prescription drug: Its active ingredient, sildenafil, has been evaluated in clinical trials for safety, effectiveness, dosing and manufacturing quality for an approved medical use.

After a dietary supplement goes to market, the FDA periodically inspects its manufacturing facilities and collects and tests some products. But it does not routinely test every supplement on store shelves. Instead, the agency prioritizes products associated with illnesses or injuries and those suspected of containing fraudulent, adulterated or otherwise illegal ingredients.
Hidden Viagra – and much more

Sildenafil and tadalafil, the active ingredients in Viagra and Cialis, belong to a class of medications called phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors. They are effective treatments for erectile dysfunction when appropriately prescribed.

But consuming these drugs unknowingly is very different from taking them under medical supervision. They are known to interact with nitrate medications, including nitroglycerin used by some people with heart disease. The combination can produce a dangerous drop in blood pressure.

The Rhino 7S case presented an additional risk: undeclared acetaminophen. It was not clear why acetaminophen was present in the supplement or how it got there. Someone taking the supplement while also using Tylenol, cold medicine or other acetaminophen-containing products could unknowingly exceed recommended amounts. Acetaminophen overdose can cause severe liver injury and, in extreme cases, acute liver failure or death.

Research suggests that adulteration is not limited to a handful of recognizable drug ingredients. A 2023 scientific review identified 112 unapproved phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and related compounds that had been detected as adulterants in sexual enhancement products between 2003 and mid-2023. Adulterated supplements can contain approved drugs, unapproved analogues and other modified compounds.
This is not solely an American problem. Studies have identified undeclared erectile dysfunction drugs in supplements sold in Europe, Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere.

In one study of 158 sexual enhancement supplements available in the United Arab Emirates, researchers found undeclared sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil in more than 12% of all sexual enhancement products they tested.

The World Health Organization has warned that increasingly complex international supply chains and the growth of e-commerce make controlling substandard and falsified health products particularly difficult. The makers of these products might source their ingredients from one country, manufacture or package them in another and sell them online to a consumer thousands of miles away.

Illicit international pharmaceutical commerce is a major problem worldwide. From December 2024 to May 2025, the international law enforcement body Interpol conducted Operation Pangea XVII, in which authorities in 90 countries seized more than 50 million doses of illicit pharmaceuticals. Erectile dysfunction medications were the second-most commonly seized product type, behind psychostimulants, which are drugs that affect how the brain regulates dopamine.

The following year, another international law enforcement operation disrupted roughly 13,000 websites, social media pages and channels and automated bots connected to illicit medicine sales. Erectile dysfunction medications were again among the most frequently seized products.

But identifying one dangerous product does not eliminate the broader market. Packaging can change. Products can disappear and reappear under new names. Sellers can move from one website or social media account to another. Manufacturers can also alter chemical ingredients.

Researchers who tracked a sexual enhancement supplement marketed as “POWER” from 2007 through 2022 found phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors in every version they tested, but the specific adulterants changed over time. Despite warnings and seizures by European food and health authorities, the product was still being sold online at the end of the study period.

Laboratory testing of supplements is therefore essential, but testing alone cannot solve the problem. Even the FDA acknowledges that its public warning list represents only a fraction of contaminated products being sold. In other words, a product’s absence from the FDA database should not be interpreted as evidence that it is safe.
Words such as “natural,” “herbal” or “dietary supplement” signal to consumers that a sexual enhancement product does not contain pharmaceutical ingredients. But that is not necessarily the case.

U.S. law requires a specific FDA disclaimer when supplement manufacturers make claims about function, but it does not require sexual enhancement supplements to carry a warning explaining that “natural” or “herbal” products may contain undeclared pharmaceutical ingredients. FDA labeling rules are therefore not designed to warn consumers specifically about hidden drugs in these products.

Online sales add another layer of complexity. Under federal law, some online marketplaces must verify identifying information from certain high-volume third-party sellers and provide consumers with a mechanism for reporting suspicious marketplace activity. But the law does not generally require marketplaces to test dietary supplements for hidden pharmaceutical ingredients or proactively report every potentially adulterated product to the FDA.

The appeal of these products is easy to understand: They offer a private, convenient and widely available solution to problems that many men find embarrassing to talk about. But that convenience can obscure a basic problem — consumers may have no reliable way to know whether the ingredients listed on the package match what is inside.

For sexual health products in particular, reducing that uncertainty will depend not only on regulation and surveillance, but also on making conversations about sexual health feel routine enough that people have safer places to turn for help.
The Conversation reached out to RhinoPills for comment, and they did not respond.

articles.title: I teach doctors how to interpret test results – and the labels ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ often hide what matters most
articles.author: Amiran Baduashvili, Associate Professor of Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: Mr. V felt tightness across his chest. His deepest breaths felt shallow. He sought help at an emergency department, where a resident physician found several worrying signs, including swelling of his hands and legs as well as heart enlargement on a chest X-ray.
Everything seemed to point to one diagnosis: heart failure, where the heart’s inability to pump blood efficiently causes fluid to build up in the body. But one result did not fit.

To diagnose heart failure, doctors often check blood levels of a hormone called BNP, which the heart releases under strain. Mr. V’s BNP levels came back normal. The resident remembered learning that BNP can be falsely normal in patients with obesity or who are overweight, even when they have heart failure. With that in mind, he dismissed the normal BNP result and ordered a diuretic to help Mr. V shed excess fluid – standard treatment for heart failure.

But Mr. V did not feel any better. The next day, a colleague of mine who was supervising the medical team examined him with an ultrasound and made a diagnosis that had been overlooked: cardiac tamponade, a life-threatening condition in which a build-up of fluid in the sac surrounding the heart compresses it so tightly that it can barely pump.

A squeezed heart needs more blood running through it, not less, so the diuretic could have been fatal. Luckily, his heart held on long enough for doctors to rush him to an operating room and drain the fluid, saving his life. Could this close call have been avoided?
The resident was right: Many patients with heart failure and excess body fat do have normal BNP levels. However, “normal” is not as simple as it sounds.

Doctors generally consider BNP values under 100 picograms per milliliter, or pg/mL, to be normal. Patients with excess weight and heart failure often have a BNP below 100, but usually not by much. A BNP value under 50 is uncommon in heart failure, even in very overweight patients. Mr. V’s BNP was 14.

This result was not just normal. It was so low that it argued strongly against a diagnosis of heart failure. But the label “normal” treated a BNP of 14 the same as a BNP of 95, hiding the very information that could have prompted doctors to look for another explanation for Mr. V’s symptoms.

Mr. V’s case reveals a deeper flaw in how doctors are trained to interpret lab results. Buried inside the word “normal” is key information that tells doctors how strongly a test result argues against a diagnosis. Some normal results can make a diagnosis slightly less likely, while others may effectively rule it out.

As a physician who studies and teaches how best to interpret diagnostic tests, I often wonder: If a test result carries so much nuanced information, why do some doctors settle for a simple “normal” or “abnormal” reading instead?
When ‘normal’ isn’t normal

The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law by President Barack Obama in 2016, gave patients greater access to their own healthcare information. Through online portals, people can often view their test results before a clinician has the chance to review them.

Those results usually come paired with a simple cutoff separating “normal” from “abnormal.” Although there are benefits to transparency, there is also a hidden cost: false alarm from “abnormal” results, and false reassurance from “normal” ones.

When I teach clinicians how to interpret diagnostic results, many are surprised to learn that, for numerous tests, mildly abnormal results may lower the likelihood of the disease they’re used to diagnose.

Take D-dimer, a blood test that doctors often order to determine whether patients with chest pain or difficulty breathing have a blood clot. A D-dimer above 500 nanograms per milliliter, or ng/mL, is labeled abnormal. But values between 500 and 1,000 actually slightly decrease the odds of a blood clot. For those at low risk for blood clots, a result in that range is nearly as reassuring as a “normal” one, even though it’s flagged as abnormal on the report. The reverse can also be true.

Cholesterol is another example. Laboratories consider levels of LDL, or “bad” cholesterol, under 100 milligrams per deciliter, or mg/dL, to be normal. However, for patients who have already suffered a heart attack or stroke, anything above 55 is too high.

Sorting results into normal and abnormal categories has a certain appeal. It makes interpreting tests easy and fast. It also reduces uncertainty. However, human biology is far from simple, and a lot of nuances are lost in that simplification.

The exact value of a test result tells doctors far more than the mere labels “normal” or “abnormal” can. Imagine a blood pressure machine that simply gave a reading of “elevated” or a heart rate monitor that read “low” instead of specific numbers. Doctors would never use such imprecise tools. Yet they often do when it comes to diagnostic tests.
Patients should feel empowered to ask their clinicians what a specific number means for them. A “normal” or “abnormal” label is a starting point for a conversation, not the final word.

My colleagues and I conducted a study that asked a simple question: What if, alongside each lab value, doctors saw not just a cutoff value for normal, but also how strongly each value points toward – or away from – a diagnosis?
We call this metric an interval likelihood ratio. It tells doctors how much a test result should raise or lower the odds that a patient has a specific diagnosis.

To derive these ratios, researchers run a test in many patients with and without the diagnosis the test is designed to pick up. Rather than drawing a single line between “normal” and “abnormal,” researchers divide the results into ranges. Each range compares how often patients with or without the diagnosis had a result within those values.

To test whether interval likelihood ratios help improve medical decisions, we recruited more than 600 clinicians across four major U.S. academic institutions. Each participant was asked to read two scenarios like Mr. V’s and make a key decision on how to manage a patient’s case based on a lab result. Everyone saw the exact test value. We randomly assigned some participants to see the numerical lab value alongside the standard cutoff for a normal result, and others to see it alongside interval likelihood ratios.
The difference between how these groups performed was not trivial.

Clinicians assigned to see interval likelihood ratios made a correct call 93 out of 100 times, while those seeing a single cutoff got it right 82 times out of 100. In other words, for roughly 1 in 10 patients like Mr. V, doctors could make a better decision if shown the degree to which a test result changes the odds of a particular diagnosis compared to merely seeing a cutoff for the normal range.
Improving how test results are displayed could help patients make better sense of their own results, help clinicians avoid critical mistakes and help health systems deliver safer care.
Clinicians learn to understand the degree to which a particular test result is abnormal through experience, shaping their intuition as they review new test results. However, intuition can be wrong.

Diagnostic errors remain one of the leading causes of harm in medicine. Our study found that interval likelihood ratios helped attending physicians, residents and advanced practice providers make better decisions, regardless of how long they’ve been practicing or their training background.

There is a legal dimension to how test results are labeled. A result flagged “abnormal” can feel like it obligates a clinician to act, such as ordering another scan, even when their own judgment says otherwise. Interval likelihood ratios can change that calculus, providing clinicians a documented, evidence-based reason to hold off ordering advanced tests and potentially saving their patients from the health risks they may entail.

The challenge is how and where to find high-quality research studies to derive interval likelihood ratios when electronic health records display only binary cutoffs as aids to interpreting test result values. It is also important to note that our study showed clinicians made better decisions in simulated scenarios, which is not the same as making decisions with real patients. The next step is testing whether these gains hold up in everyday practice, across different institutions, care settings and lab tests.
Test results are more than normal or abnormal. For patients like Mr. V, the difference between these labels and the numbers behind them can be the difference between life and death.
Amiran Baduashvili is the founder of EBM Clarity, Inc, which owns an online course in diagnostic reasoning. His earns no income from this endeavor.

articles.title: When abortion and surrogacy law collide, contracts can’t answer the hardest questions
articles.author: Sonia Suter, Professor of Law, George Washington University
paras: Surrogacy arrangements – agreements for someone to carry a pregnancy for the intended parents – have existed for millennia, and modern surrogacy contracts for half a century.

These contracts typically address parental rights, the possibility of abortion, medical instructions, health insurance and payment of expenses, each side with its own legal representation. The contracts are usually honored, resulting in thousands of babies born through surrogacy in the U.S., at a cost that can top US$200,000 when agencies are involved.

In a 2026 case, surrogate McKenna West refused the intended parents’ request for an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart condition. The case raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the surrogate’s bodily autonomy collides with the intended parents’ wishes?

As scholars of reproductive justice and family law, we see this case as an example of how rapidly changing abortion laws, reproductive technology and family law can create conflicts that surrogacy contracts cannot necessarily anticipate.

West’s contract stated that “there shall be a termination of the pregnancy for a fetal abnormality … if the Intended Parents request” it. She later wrote that “their lawyer and my own former lawyer sent me letters threatening six-figure penalties if I didn’t comply with their demand to terminate.”

Instead, West moved from Alaska to Texas, where she had family support and believed the baby, when born, could get needed care. Moreover, she knew that Texas bans abortion in almost all circumstances. Meanwhile, the intended parents, who lived in California, obtained a court order before the birth stating they would become the legal parents once the baby was born.

Before West gave birth, the Texas attorney general obtained a court order requiring lifesaving care for the baby, stating that “the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the lifesaving surgery.” West sought custody but was willing to drop her claims if the couple agreed to the baby’s treatment.

After the Texas courts upheld the intended parents’ rights, West asked the Supreme Court to intervene so she could receive “further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” The court declined, leaving West no rights to the baby.

In a similar 2012 case, surrogate Crystal Kelley signed a contract allowing the intended parents to call for an abortion in case of a severe fetal abnormality. When the fetus was diagnosed with a heart defect and other serious anomalies, the parents asked Kelley to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and left Connecticut, where she would not have had parental rights, for Michigan, which at the time would treat her as the legal mother. Kelley placed the baby for adoption, and the girl’s adoptive parents raised her until her death at 8.

In the 1988 Baby M case, a surrogate who was also the genetic mother insisted she should be the mother despite signing a contract to relinquish parental rights. The New Jersey Supreme Court voided that contract because it held that she could not give up her parental rights before birth. As a result, it recognized the surrogate as the legal mother but awarded custody to the father. She later received visitation rights.
A state-by-state patchwork
Surrogacy contracts establishing legal parentage are enforceable in a number of states. But surrogacy laws vary by state, creating a patchwork with respect to enforceability.

West’s journey, for example, involved three states – Alaska, Texas and the intended parents’ state of California. They are deemed surrogacy-friendly, meaning contracts are relatively easy to enforce there, though the states diverge sharply on abortion.

Surrogacy agreements may require the surrogate to restrict travel, eat nutritiously and cooperate with healthcare providers. As in the West and Kelley cases, agreements may also specify when the surrogate could be asked to abort or, if pregnant with multiple fetuses, selectively terminate.
These abortion provisions have rarely been tested in court, and West’s case hasn’t resolved whether they are enforceable. Rather, they raise the question: Can anyone be forced to have an abortion?

After the Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which held there is no fundamental right to abortion, states have determined their own abortion laws. In states like Texas, abortion provisions in surrogacy contracts are unenforceable. But even where abortion is legal, a court would likely refuse to compel an abortion, given the surrogate’s bodily autonomy.
A surrogate’s control over her body may be more limited, however, when intended parents seek to enforce provisions meant to protect the fetus.

If a physician recommends a C-section for the fetus’s well-being and the surrogate refuses, for example, a court might enforce a contract clause requiring her “to cooperate with her medical providers.”
Even before 2022, when abortion was still a federal constitutional right, courts in some – but not all – jurisdictions ordered C-sections against the pregnant person’s wishes.
In other words, bodily autonomy has never been absolute for pregnant people.
Since Dobbs, surrogacy and abortion have become increasingly intertwined.

In 2025, a Florida judge questioned the constitutionality of surrogacy on fetal-personhood grounds – the legal theory that an unborn fetus or embryo has the same legal rights as a born human – even as he granted the intended parents parental rights.

In his view, there can be no “contractual ownership interest over the unborn baby.” Florida’s attorney general took the argument further, declaring that the couple’s contract with the surrogate violated the 13th Amendment’s ban on slavery. A spokesperson said he was concerned “about any case where a surrogacy company profits off the sale of children.”

Some conservative legislators and advocacy groups have also been challenging the legitimacy of surrogacy, a few with plans to limit or even ban it. Consequently, in states that take fetal and embryo personhood seriously, surrogacy contracts and even IVF could become unavailable.

West’s case has surfaced starkly different views of what is at stake. For some, surrogacy is a form of baby selling that should not be allowed. For others, it is a way for intended parents to create families and for surrogates to support them.

Surrogacy asks the law to recognize both the interests of people who intend to become parents and the autonomy of the person who is pregnant. Dobbs has made that balance harder to maintain by inviting fetal-personhood principles into areas of law that had not previously treated fetuses or embryos as persons.
